nameStory: The club-gilled nudibranch gets its name from the distinctive club-shaped projections on its back called cerata, which function like external gills. These finger-like structures help the tiny sea slug breathe underwater while also giving it a spiky, otherworldly appearance that makes it look like a miniature underwater cactus.
description: The club-gilled nudibranch is a tiny sea slug that crawls along the ocean floor and underwater surfaces. These translucent marine creatures are usually pale or whitish in color and rarely grow larger than a fingernail. Like all nudibranchs (pronounced NEW-dih-branks), they're shell-less snails that breathe through external gills and feed by grazing on small organisms. Their delicate, almost ethereal appearance makes them popular subjects for underwater photographers.

idTips.label: Club-shaped cerata
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive finger-like projections on the back that are swollen at the tips like tiny clubs - these are the external gills that give this species its name

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: Body appears translucent white to pale cream, sometimes with a subtle pinkish or yellowish tinge visible through the thin skin

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Typically no larger than your thumbnail, often much smaller - you'll need to look closely or use magnification to see details

idTips.label: Smooth body texture
idTips.description: Body feels soft and gelatinous to the touch, like a tiny piece of firm jelly, with no shell or hard parts

idTips.label: Two tentacles
idTips.description: Head bears two horn-like projections called rhinophores that the animal uses to smell and taste the water around it

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, typically on rocky substrates, pilings, and among seaweed in the intertidal and subtidal zones. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are often discovered clinging to algae, hydroids, or the undersides of rocks during low tide. Look for them in tide pools, on dock pilings, or while snorkeling in eelgrass beds.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to warm. Best time to find them in shallow tide pools during extreme low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be found feeding and reproducing. Look for them on dock pilings and in shallow, protected waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper water as temperatures cool. Continue checking tide pools and rocky areas.
seasonality.winter: Least active period - they may retreat to deeper water or become dormant, making them very difficult to find in shallow areas.

funFact: Club-gilled nudibranchs can actually steal and use the stinging cells from the hydroids they eat, incorporating them into their own skin as a defense mechanism - essentially turning their prey's weapons into their own personal security system!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small, pale nudibranchs, but the distinctive club-shaped tips on the gill projections are the key differentiator. Remember: if the 'fingers' on the back are swollen at the tips like tiny drumsticks, you've found a club-gilled nudibranch.
contextualKnowledge: Nudibranchs are often called 'sea slugs' but they're actually more closely related to snails than to garden slugs. The name 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills' in Latin, referring to their external breathing structures that are visible on their backs.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like the minute aeolis, the club-gilled nudibranch has more distinctly club-shaped cerata rather than pointed ones. While Eubranchus scintillans may have similar body structure, the club-gilled variety's cerata are notably more swollen at the tips and the overall coloration tends to be paler and more translucent.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The sparkling nudibranch differs from its relatives by having distinctly club-shaped rhinophores and cerata arranged in tight clusters rather than rows.
The Minute Aeolis is much smaller than its relative the club-gilled nudibranch (Eubranchus pallidus), which grows larger and has more club-shaped rather than finger-like cerata.
